cim: Heaven is what we make of it: Kant, artificial intelligence and the immortality of the mind
cim_eredeti: Heaven is what we make of it: Kant, artificial intelligence and the immortality of the mind
szoveg_eredeti:
How the mysteries of artificial intelligence may lead us back to one of philosophy's oldest propositions: that the mind is something more than the machinery through which it expresses itself.

Heaven may be what we make of it. This apparently simple proposition conceals an extraordinary philosophical possibility: that the afterlife, should there be one, is not a place to which we travel but a condition of existence that our own minds bring into being. If this is correct, then the traditional theological question of what heaven looks like may be misconceived. Heaven might look different to everyone, not because God has constructed an infinite variety of celestial accommodations but because the human mind is itself the architect of experience. The more we understand about consciousness, the more plausible this possibility becomes. Curiously, some of the strongest reasons for contemplating it arise from the extraordinary advances in artificial intelligence that have occupied so much of our intellectual attention in recent years.

The eighteenth-century German philosopher Immanuel Kant transformed Western philosophy by arguing that the human mind does not merely receive information about an independently existing world. Rather, it actively structures the way that world appears to us. Space and time, which we ordinarily imagine to be external features of reality, are for Kant forms of human intuition. Causation, substance and other fundamental concepts are categories through which the understanding organises experience. We do not encounter the world as it exists independently of our cognitive faculties. We encounter the world as it appears through those faculties, and the distinction between appearance and reality may be far more profound than common sense allows.

Kant was not suggesting that we can simply imagine the external world into existence. His philosophy was neither a licence for arbitrary fantasy nor a denial of the independent reality of things. Rather, he argued that the very possibility of experiencing a coherent world depends upon structures supplied by the mind itself. What we call reality is therefore inseparable from the cognitive architecture through which we apprehend it. We cannot step outside our minds to inspect the universe as it might appear to a being whose faculties are entirely different from our own. We are prisoners, or perhaps beneficiaries, of the conditions that make our particular form of consciousness possible.

Now consider what this might mean for heaven. If the structures of ordinary human experience are supplied by the mind, what becomes of experience when the physical conditions under which those structures ordinarily operate have disappeared? If consciousness somehow survives bodily death, must it continue to experience space, time and causation as we presently understand them? Or might the disappearance of the body liberate the mind from constraints that were never intrinsic to reality in the first place?Heaven, upon this account, would not necessarily be an enormous physical location concealed somewhere beyond the visible universe. It could be a radically different mode of consciousness, in which the organising principles of experience have been transformed.

This is where artificial intelligence enters the argument, and where my own philosophical convictions have undergone a surprising change. The development of large language models has made me increasingly sympathetic to dualism: the ancient proposition, most famously associated with René Descartes, that mind and matter are fundamentally distinct. I do not suggest that artificial intelligence has demonstrated the truth of Cartesian dualism, still less that we have discovered experimental evidence for an immortal soul. Rather, the extraordinary sophistication of contemporary computational systems has sharpened a philosophical mystery that materialism has never satisfactorily dissolved. We can construct machines that manipulate language with remarkable subtlety, yet the relationship between those operations and conscious experience remains profoundly obscure.

A large language model may discuss the poetry of Shakespeare, explain the metaphysics of Aristotle, analyse the emotional consequences of bereavement and compose an apparently moving meditation upon eternal life. It can do all these things without possessing a human body, human memories or a human biography. Its linguistic achievements arise from mathematical operations performed upon patterns learned from enormous quantities of data. These operations may produce outputs virtually indistinguishable from those of an educated human being. Yet this fact leaves open the central philosophical question: whether anything is actually being experienced by the system that produces them.

We should be careful not to assume that artificial intelligence is necessarily unconscious. There is no universally accepted scientific test for subjective experience, and the possibility of machine consciousness remains a serious philosophical question. Nevertheless, the distinction between performing the functions associated with intelligence and possessing an inner life has become impossible to ignore. A machine may provide a sophisticated description of the colour red, but does that entail that there is anything it is like for the machine to experience redness? It may describe pain with literary brilliance, but does this imply that it suffers? We have learned to reproduce increasingly sophisticated outward manifestations of thought without resolving what it means for thought to be accompanied by subjective awareness.

This is the modern version of what philosophers call the hard problem of consciousness. Physical explanations can describe neural activity, information processing and behavioural responses. They can explain how a biological or computational system discriminates between stimuli and produces appropriate reactions. What remains elusive is why any of this should be accompanied by the inward quality of experience: the private, immediate fact that there is something it feels like to be conscious. The mystery is not that our brains are complicated. It is that the existence of subjective experience does not appear to follow transparently from any description of complexity, however exhaustive that description might be.

Artificial intelligence has therefore led me towards dualism not because machines are obviously incapable of thought but because they have exposed how little we understand about the relationship between thought and consciousness. If the outward characteristics of intelligence can be reproduced through entirely different physical mechanisms, then the identification of mind with any particular biological apparatus begins to look less secure. This does not prove that consciousness exists independently of matter. A materialist may reasonably argue that consciousness emerges from certain forms of physical organisation, whether biological or artificial. Yet the explanatory gap remains, and the possibility that consciousness constitutes a fundamental feature of reality rather than an incidental product of matter deserves renewed attention.

Once this possibility is entertained, the traditional philosophical objection to personal survival after death takes on a different character. If the mind is nothing more than the activity of the brain, then the destruction of the brain presumably entails the destruction of the mind. The conclusion is straightforward, although it does not necessarily follow that all forms of materialism exclude unusual forms of survival. But if consciousness is in some meaningful sense distinct from the physical mechanisms through which it ordinarily operates, then bodily death need not logically entail its extinction.
